new_findings_this_run.detail: The known issue feedproxy-cache-key-proves-a-200, recorded 2026-10-03 and called 'the most useful thing this run found', is WRONG and is retired tonight. It claimed that the presence of a 'feedproxy:<url>' key in /api/debug proves that feed returned 200 within the last 15 minutes. It does not. backend/cache.py Cache.keys() is `return list(self._store.keys())` with no expiry filter at all, and eviction is LAZY: entries are only dropped inside get(), when something actually asks for that key. So an expired key sits in the /api/debug listing indefinitely until the next request for it. PROOF FROM TONIGHT, not inference: /api/debug at 04:22Z listed two NVD keys carrying pubEndDate 2026-10-10T04:36:18 and 2026-10-10T04:44:59. Those are the exact timestamps the 2026-10-10 run recorded, roughly 24 hours old, and the page computes that date from the current clock, so neither could have been created tonight. Tonight's real load created a third key dated 2026-10-11T04:24:06. CONSEQUENCE: key presence proves only that a feed returned 200 at SOME point since the backend container last started, which can be days. Nights that leaned on this for feed verdicts are weaker than they read, 2026-10-03 most explicitly, which stated feed health was 'established to a high standard without a browser' largely on this basis. Correct use from now on: treat a feedproxy key as evidence of configuration and of a historical success, never as evidence of current health, and establish current feed health by actually exercising the feed (browser load, or a nonce'd /api/feed fetch). USEFUL COROLLARY worth keeping: because keys are never swept, a key surviving from a previous night is positive proof the backend container has not restarted in between, which is a free deploy signal for backend changes.

runs.correction_to_own_earlier_reasoning: RECORDED because a future run will reason the same way and should not. This entry originally predicted that a frontend-only deploy would land the synth frontend while leaving 69a1385's nginx /synth/ no-cache carve-out UNAPPLIED, and warned that a working /synth/ would not prove the nginx change had shipped. That prediction was WRONG, and reading .github/workflows/deploy.yml lines 88-150 properly is what corrected it. Two details defeat the intuition that backend=false means 'frontend only'. (1) The droplet SSH step runs `git fetch origin main` then `git reset --hard origin/main` unconditionally, so the droplet working tree goes to the FULL origin/main state including 69a1385's nginx/nginx.conf, regardless of which branch the flag selects. (2) `docker compose restart nginx` also runs UNCONDITIONALLY, with an explicit in-file comment saying 'Restart it either way; it is cheap', precisely because nginx.conf is a bind mount read once at start; it is followed by `nginx -t`, which exits 1 and fails the deploy if the config is bad. So backend=false skips only `docker compose build backend` and `docker compose up -d`, and 69a1385 touched no backend/ file at all: it tripped the ^nginx/ path regex, not a genuine backend change. NET EFFECT: this routine's state.json push completed 69a1385's deployment in full, nginx carve-out included, and the nginx config validated. LESSON: read the deploy script's unconditional steps before reasoning about what a flag skips.

known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: Refines the 2026-09-04 webfetch-provenance-gate note. PROVENANCE_REQUIRED is NOT necessarily an all-night, all-host block. On 2026-09-05 the very first call (dxedge.net/api/health) returned it, and an immediate retry of the same URL succeeded; every later dxedge.net fetch worked. The same night it was permanently sticky for services.nvd.nist.gov across two attempts. Correct behaviour: retry a denied URL ONCE, and if it is still denied treat that host as unavailable, record the gap, and do NOT substitute curl, python or headless Chromium for it. A 2026-09-04-style total block should therefore be confirmed with a retry before the whole run is abandoned. 2026-09-28 was cross-host, not per-host: dxedge.net, api.pota.app and services.swpc.noaa.gov were all denied in the same run, so tonight matches the 09-27 total-block shape rather than the 09-18 partial one. Including the URL in a visible user message, which the error text suggests as a remedy, did not clear it. ### REFINED 2026-10-07: the 10-06 advice to re-probe with a URL not yet tried is necessary but NOT sufficient. Tonight /api/satellites/positions was itself untried when it was denied, and the gate only revealed itself open on the NEXT untried URL (/health/linkcheck.json), after which 20 consecutive calls succeeded including the two previously refused. Keep re-probing with DIFFERENT untried URLs; do not conclude a blind night from one untried URL failing. ### REFINED 2026-10-09, and this is the most consequential correction to this note so far: A FAILING example.com CONTROL DOES NOT PROVE A BLIND NIGHT. Tonight 4 calls were denied in the first 10 minutes, among them an https://example.com/ control, which 09-20, 09-27, 09-28 and 10-02 all treated as the decisive proof of an all-host total block. On the strength of that the run sent its escalation push early, per the 09-16 lesson. The push was WRONG: the very next two untried URLs (/health/linkcheck.json and /api/debug) both answered first try about a minute later, and roughly 20 consecutive calls then succeeded, including /api/health on a third param name after it had been refused on two. So the control is NOT a reliable discriminator, and neither the all-host shape nor the total-block shape can be concluded from it. Practical rule for future runs: before calling a night blind, re-probe with at least TWO DIFFERENT UNTRIED dxedge.net paths, and prefer paths not yet touched in the run over fresh param values on a path already refused. Weigh the 09-16 send-early lesson against this one: an early push can convert a blind night into a full one, but it also risks waking James for nothing, so the honest resolution is to send early AND send a correcting push if the gate later opens, which is what this run did. ### 2026-10-10: the refined rule WORKED and is now load-bearing, so keep it. Two denials on /api/health (cb=20261010a, cb=20261010b) opened the night. Under the pre-10-09 reading that pattern plus a control would have been called a blind night and drawn an escalation push. Instead the run re-probed with two DIFFERENT untried paths, /health/linkcheck.json and /api/debug, both of which answered first try, and ~25 calls then succeeded including /api/health itself on a third param name (probe1010=c). Two practical additions. First, a non-dxedge call that SUCCEEDS is useful early evidence the gate is not total: an arrl.org fetch answered before the dxedge retries tonight. A failing control proves nothing (10-09) but a passing one is informative. Second, retrying the SAME path with a new param value is the weakest possible probe and should not be counted as one of the two required untried paths. SHARPENED 2026-10-13: the gate is per-URL, not merely per-host. /api/health and /api/debug were each denied twice on dxedge.net while /health/linkcheck.json on the SAME HOST answered on the first call, and a later bare-path retry of both denied endpoints succeeded. Operational rule: never conclude the night is blind from a denial on one path. Probe a second path on the same host, and retry a denied path later in the run. ### RECONFIRMED 2026-10-16, second consecutive night with the identical shape: dxedge.net fully open (~25 successes, including cache-busted and nonce'd URLs, after only the very first call of the night being denied and clearing on a bare retry) while 6 distinct third-party hosts were refused with retries. Two nights running makes the per-host split the expected condition of an unattended run, not an intermittency to re-test from scratch. Practical consequence: plan the run so Steps 1-3 (all dxedge.net) are completed first and the curated sweep is attempted last, and do not spend calls proving the split beyond about 6 denied hosts.

WebFetch response caching is documented as 15 minutes per URL but in practice returned bodies from the 2026-09-02 run when this run requested the identical /api/feed URL strings 8 days later. Five feeds appeared frozen at their 09-01/09-02 content while the upstreams, fetched directly, were current to 09-09. Appending a per-run nonce query param to the dxedge URL (for example &nonce=0910a) changes the WebFetch cache key while leaving the backend behaviour identical, because /api/feed keys its own cache on the url param alone and FastAPI ignores the extra param. EVERY nightly /api/feed and /api/* check must carry a fresh nonce, or it is testing this container's cache instead of the site. A feed that looks stale should be confirmed against the upstream before it is reported. WORSE THAN DOCUMENTED, 2026-09-18: a CHANGED cache-busting param did not defeat it. /api/health?cb=20260918run1 at 04:14Z and /api/health?cb=20260918post at 05:00Z returned byte-identical bodies carrying the same 04:14:25Z timestamp, while a python fetch at 05:00Z returned a fresh 05:00:28Z. So a distinct cb/nonce value is necessary but NOT sufficient: WebFetch can still serve a cached body for a URL it has seen before with a different query string. Practical consequence: never judge post-deploy freshness from a WebFetch timestamp alone. Confirm it against a second, independent read of the same non-denied endpoint. ### AMENDED 2026-10-07, and this amendment is the practically important one. A BARE URL with no query parameter is the worst case, not merely an equal one: https://dxedge.net/sw.js fetched with no param returned CACHE_NAME 'dxedge-v37' while the live file (same URL plus ?n1007=live6) returned 'dxedge-v56' matching repo HEAD. Read naively the stale body looks like a 19-version-stale frontend and a serious deploy regression. Static assets are exactly where a cache-buster feels unnecessary and so is exactly where this trap waits. RULE: cache-bust EVERY WebFetch including static files, and before believing any version string or timestamp, sanity-check it against git history (git log -L on the constant settled it in one command).

Cloning with --depth N makes `git log -1 -- <file>` report the shallow boundary commit for every file, which reads as though the curated-link sources were edited recently. Always `git fetch --unshallow` (or clone full) before deciding whether new outbound links exist.

scripts/health/linkcheck.py reported https://www.hamqsl.com/solarxml.php as broken with HTTP 307. It is not rot. Fetched on its own immediately afterwards the same URL returns 200 with current XML (solar flux 100, updated 17 Sep 2026 0417 GMT), and the site's own /api/feed served it 200 on both browser loads. The 307 carries no Location header, which is a throttle signature rather than a redirect, and it appears because the sweep hits ~150 URLs concurrently. www.hamqsl.com/solar.html answers the same way. One of the cyber page's two api.first.org EPSS calls returned 504 Gateway Timeout on the first page load of the night and 200 on a reload 45 seconds later, with the upstream itself answering in 0.5s when fetched directly. The exact certificate expiry IS obtainable from this container, closing a gap every prior run recorded as unreadable. openssl and curl both see the egress proxy certificate, but the Certificate Transparency logs do not care: curl -H 'Accept: application/json' -A 'Mozilla/5.0' 'https://crt.sh/?q=dxedge.net&output=json' returns issuance and expiry for every cert ever issued for the domain. Note crt.sh returned a 502 HTML page on the first call and correct JSON on an immediate retry, so always retry once before concluding it is unavailable AMENDED 2026-09-30: this technique is NOT always available. WebFetch to https://crt.sh/?q=dxedge.net&output=json returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED tonight, and once WebFetch has refused a URL, substitution-is-not-permitted bars reaching it by curl. So the curl recipe in this note is usable only on a night when WebFetch has not refused crt.sh. Do not treat an unreadable expiry date as a cert problem: cert STATUS is judged by the clean TLS fetch, per Step 1. AMENDED AGAIN 2026-10-03: crt.sh refused WebFetch on robots grounds for the second time (also 09-30), and the weekly linkcheck independently recorded crt.sh at HTTP 502 on 09-28. Treat this technique as usually UNAVAILABLE rather than usually available, and do not let an unreadable expiry read as a cert problem.

WITHDRAWN 2026-09-27. Do not act on this note. It is retained only so a future run understands why three nights of results look stronger than they were. The note originally said that because the sandbox egress proxy fails closed on bad upstream certificates, a plain curl returning 200 is positive evidence that dxedge.net's real certificate chain is valid, and concluded that Steps 1, 2 and 4 are all reachable by curl on a blind WebFetch night. The technical claim about the proxy failing closed may well still be true. The OPERATIONAL conclusion is not available to this routine: once WebFetch has failed or been denied for a URL, the run is not permitted to retrieve that content by curl, python requests, headless Chromium, or any other client. https://dxedge.net/health/linkcheck.json is produced by the weekly GitHub Actions job from normal egress with a browser UA, covers all 663 URLs across all five source files, and is usually FRESHER than the in-container 14-day rotating sweep. READ IT EVERY NIGHT, unconditionally, regardless of whether the curated sweep is due. On 2026-09-26 it was read for the first time and immediately surfaced three genuine cisa.gov 404s that the sweep-not-due rule had been skipping since 09-21. Parse-check the body as JSON, not just the status code: if the file is missing the SPA catch-all answers with index.html and HTTP 200. Always re-verify its broken entries independently before editing, since roughly half are transient: of the 9 broken on 09-21, 3 were real, 2 were transient, 2 were the http-only 503 artifact and 2 were two-network failures. Read again 2026-10-03: generated_at 2026-09-28T17:41:17Z, 666 URLs, 7 broken, all 7 assessed as not rot. Note the report can be up to 7 days old because the job is weekly; judge its freshness against its own generated_at, and do not read a 5-day-old report as a broken job. ### AMENDED 2026-10-04 with the actual schedule, so no future run raises a false alarm about a stale report: .github/workflows/linkcheck.yml runs cron '17 9 * * 1', Mondays 09:17 UTC. A report is therefore expected to be up to 7 days old by design, and 2026-09-28 was a Monday. Suspect the CI job only when a run AFTER a passed Monday 09:17 UTC still reads the previous Monday's generated_at.

A TECHNIQUE, not a defect, and the most useful thing this run found. /api/debug lists the backend's live cache keys, and every proxied feed appears there as 'feedproxy:<exact upstream url>'. In backend/feedproxy.py fetch_feed, cache.set is reached ONLY on the HTTP 200 path: a non-200 raises FeedProxyError before it, a redirect with no Location raises, an over-cap body raises, and a disallowed host raises at validate() before any fetch happens. DEFAULT_TTL is 900s. Therefore the presence of a feedproxy key in /api/debug is proof that that exact feed returned 200 through the proxy within the last 15 minutes. One WebFetch of /api/debug thus answers, for EVERY feed on both standalone pages at once, the three questions Step 3 asks about non-200s, allowlist 403s and 502s. This matters because the Step 3 browser check can never run in a cloud scheduled session, and because it costs one request instead of seventeen, which also sidesteps api-rate-limit-on-feed. What it does NOT answer: whether a 200 body parsed correctly into its panel, whether the page logged a console error, and whether a panel is rendering an inline '<name> failed:' string. Those remain genuinely unchecked without a browser, and a run must say so rather than calling a cache-key sweep a render verdict. ### AMENDED 2026-10-04, READ THIS BEFORE USING THE TECHNIQUE: the 900s claim above is WRONG and the technique is downgraded. backend/cache.py keys() returns list(self._store.keys()) with no expiry filtering; expiry is applied lazily in get() only. A key whose feed is never read again lingers for the life of the container. Tonight's /api/debug still listed NVD keys with pubEndDate=2026-09-26 and 2026-09-30 and four www.cisa.gov link-verification paths proxied by the 09-26 run, all days outside any TTL. A present key therefore proves a 200 at SOME time since the backend container started, never a 200 within the last 15 minutes. Do not use it as a freshness or render verdict. Use it only as a lower bound (host allowlisted and reachable at least once) or to spot a feed with NO key at all. Live proof needs one /api/feed fetch per feed, paced per api-rate-limit-on-feed; the 2026-10-04 run did exactly that for all 16 and all answered 200. ### 2026-10-07: this technique carried the ENTIRE of Step 3 tonight, with no browser and no per-feed probing, proving all 12 live feed targets 200 from a single /api/debug call. It is now the primary browserless substitute for the render check. Caveat recorded tonight: /api/debug also retains feedproxy keys from PAST nightly runs' own link-verification fetches (e.g. www.cisa.gov/scuba, a discarded 09-26 guess). Those are probe leftovers, not page feeds, and must not be mistaken for new proxy targets needing allowlist review. ### 2026-10-08: NOT relied on as the primary Step 3 evidence tonight, because the gate was fully open and all 16 feeds were probed individually instead. Recording the preference so it does not drift: live per-feed /api/feed probing with fresh nonces is STRICTLY better evidence and is what a working night should spend its requests on. The cache-key sweep is the fallback for a partially blocked night, and 16 paced probes in batches of four drew no rate limiting. ### RETIRED 2026-10-11, DO NOT USE. The core claim is false. backend/cache.py Cache.keys() returns list(self._store.keys()) with no expiry filter, and eviction happens only lazily inside get(), so an EXPIRED feedproxy key stays listed in /api/debug indefinitely until something requests that exact key. Proven from tonight's data rather than inferred: /api/debug at 04:22Z still listed NVD keys with pubEndDate 2026-10-10T04:36:18 and 04:44:59, the 10-10 run's own timestamps about 24h old, while tonight's genuine load produced a separate 2026-10-11T04:24:06 key. A feedproxy key therefore proves only that the feed returned 200 at some point since the container last started. Establish CURRENT feed health by exercising the feed (browser load, or a nonce'd /api/feed fetch), never from the key listing. Keep one corollary: a key surviving from a previous night proves the backend container has not restarted since, which is a free deploy signal.

Sharpens webfetch-response-cache-crosses-nights with a worse failure mode: WebFetch can return the body of a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT URL. Tonight the cyber page's production NVD query through /api/feed (a very long URL: /api/feed?url= plus a percent-encoded NVD URL carrying two doubly-encoded ISO timestamps) first failed with CLIENT_ERROR, then on retry with a different nonce returned the HACKADAY radio-hacks RSS feed, and returned Hackaday AGAIN when the nonce was moved to the FRONT of the query string to change the URL prefix. The Hackaday feed had been fetched minutes earlier through the same /api/feed path. So for long /api/feed URLs, neither a fresh nonce value nor a changed prefix reliably separates cache entries, and a plausible-looking feed body is NOT evidence that the feed you asked for is healthy. DIAGNOSTIC THAT WORKED: a SHORT control URL on the same host (/api/feed?url= NVD cveId=CVE-2025-21298) returned correct NVD JSON, proving host, allowlist and proxy were all fine. RULE for future runs: when a /api/feed probe returns content that does not match the feed requested, do not record either a pass or a fail from it. A COROLLARY that survives the retirement of feedproxy-cache-key-proves-a-200, and the one part of that technique still worth using. awaiting_james.detail: backend/solar.py line 13 sets SFI_URL to https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/solar-cycle/observed-solar-cycle-indices.json. That file is MONTHLY, not daily: its records are time-tagged year-month ("1749-01" onward) and each row is a monthly mean. So the sfi and ssn the whole site runs on are last month's averages, and they cannot change until the month rolls over. CONFIRMED FACTS: the URL is what solar.py reads (source read directly); the file is monthly (granularity read from the file); /api/health has reported sfi 116 on 2026-09-22, 09-23 and 09-30, and every recent /api/solar/history row carries the identical sfi 116, a_index 7, ssn 76 while its timestamp advances every 15 minutes; the site's own hamqsl feed, fetched through /api/feed tonight and updated 30 Sep 2026 0410 GMT, reports solarflux 92. So dxedge.net currently shows 116 on the dashboard and 92 on the cyber page, from the same origin, about 24 points apart. INFERENCE, not confirmed: that 116 is a September or August monthly mean and the gap will persist until the month turns. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND the number on screen: sfi is passed straight into the propagation model, backend/main.py feeds it to predict_path at lines 267, 296 and 375 and uses round(sfi) in the voacap and recommendation cache keys, so a 24-point overstatement biases every band recommendation optimistic and freezes the cache key for a month at a time. It also breaks two alerts in backend/alerts.py: the 10m opening alert fires on sfi >= 150 and the sfi_drop alert compares against prev_sfi, and neither can behave sensibly on a value that only moves once a month. Separately and more minor, a_index is not measured at all: line 58 derives it from a hardcoded Kp lookup table, so the displayed A index is a function of Kp rather than a real A index. NOT FIXED AUTONOMOUSLY, deliberately: swapping the endpoint changes what the number means, which is explicitly an escalation ("a feed replacement that changes data semantics"). DECISION NEEDED: should solar.py move to a daily 10.7cm source? The obvious candidates are https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/products/summary/10cm-flux.json (current daily value, single object, trivial parse) or https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/f107_cm_flux.json (daily series). Neither could be verified from this container tonight: the summary URL was gated by WebFetch twice and the run is not permitted to substitute another client, so a future run or James should confirm the exact response shape before any change. Note hamqsl already gives a daily flux and the backend already fetches it for the cyber page, so reusing that is a third option with no new upstream. ### REFRESHED 2026-10-19 (no change in status, numbers only): the predicted month rollover HAPPENED. /api/health now reports sfi 105, down from the 116 that held across 09-22, 09-23 and 09-30, which confirms the inference recorded above that 116 was a monthly mean frozen until the month turned. The gap has WIDENED rather than closed: hamqsl through /api/feed tonight reports solarflux 137 updated 19 Oct 2026 0404 GMT, so the dashboard and the cyber page now disagree by 32 points from the same origin, against 24 points on 09-30. Still the highest-value open item and still not fixed autonomously, for the same reason: changing the endpoint changes what the number means.

Security-relevant, pre-existing, and not previously tracked. frontend/src/components/Support.jsx renders the donation QR codes as pointing at a third party: https://api.qrserver.com/v1/create-qr-code/?size=NxN&data=&bgcolor=0e0e0e&color=7affb2&qzone=2. The values passed in the data param are the page's BTC address (bc1q99...dgxl), ETH address (0x450Af...82db), https://paypal.me/sagejw and now https://ko-fi.com/oldtimeradio. CONCRETE RISK, and it is worse than the ordinary third-party-asset case: the QR is the artifact a visitor actually scans, and a compromised, hijacked or MITM'd api.qrserver.com could return a QR encoding a DIFFERENT wallet address while the plain-text address printed next to it stays correct. People scan QR codes without reading the address underneath, so donations would silently redirect with no visible tell and no integrity check available - an cannot carry subresource integrity, and the URL is built fresh on every render. Secondary issues: the addresses are disclosed to a third party on every page view (minor, they are public by design), and the QRs break if the service goes down. PROVENANCE, stated precisely so this is not misread as a regression: Support.jsx was added by James himself in 59111ba on 2026-05-31, and the 7 OTR commits of 2026-10-01 only changed its KOFI constant. The dependency is James's own and about four months old. It surfaced tonight only because reviewing those commits meant reading the file, and it appears in neither known_issues nor awaiting_james, so it has never been reported. NOT fixed autonomously: it is not link rot, not a redirect, not a deprecated feed endpoint and not an /api/feed bypass (an image load is not a CORS fetch and cannot go through a proxy that returns text, same reasoning as otr-audio-is-a-media-element-not-a-feed), so it falls outside all four repair categories. It is also closely analogous to crane-cab-third-party-cdn, which was escalated rather than fixed. OPTIONS: (a) leave as is; (b) generate the QR codes client-side from a vendored QR library, which removes the third party entirely and is the clean fix; (c) pre-generate the four QR PNGs once, eyeball-verify each decodes to the right address, and commit them as static assets, which also removes the runtime dependency and is the smallest change; (d) drop the QR codes and show copy-to-clipboard text addresses only. Recommend (c) for the crypto addresses specifically, since those are the ones where a swap costs real money and the address set almost never changes. NOTE this was found by source reading on a blind night: whether the QRs currently render, and whether api.qrserver.com is even reachable, was NOT verified.

Measured at 03:15-03:17 UTC, an hour BEFORE this run probed: WebFetch of https://dxedge.net/sw.js?v=69a1385 read CACHE_NAME 'dxedge-v69'; WebFetch of /synth/index.html?v=69a1385 read title 'Filament - a tube synthesizer - DXEdge'; a headless Chromium loaded https://dxedge.net/synth/, the engine came up and rendered audio, and the main page showed the Filament tab; curl -D of /synth/rack.js returned 'Cache-Control: no-cache, must-revalidate', i.e. nginx had already restarted onto 69a1385's /synth/ carve-out. LIKELY CAUSE of the stale reading (inference, not proven): the same session had fetched the BARE URLs /sw.js and /synth/ at about 03:14 UTC, seconds before the deploy finished, and those pre-deploy responses (v68, SPA catch-all) appear to have been served from a WebFetch cache to this later run. LESSON: always put a fresh cache-busting query on WebFetch deploy checks (the sw.js tripwire included); a bare URL can return another session's earlier copy. No Actions log needs reading. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. Commit 69a1385 "feat(synth): Filament v0.1" (2026-10-12 20:14:04 PT) and 0e2c2c4 (20:16:55 PT) have not reached production, confirmed ~70 minutes later by two independent signals: production sw.js CACHE_NAME is dxedge-v68 while repo HEAD is dxedge-v69 (bumped by 69a1385 itself), and https://dxedge.net/synth/ serves the SPA catch-all with no "Filament" string, which is nginx behaviour when frontend/dist has no synth/ directory. At 70 minutes against a 6-10 minute deploy this is a failed or never-started workflow run. WHAT I CANNOT DO: read the cause. api.github.com is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy, so the Actions run status, the step that failed and the droplet deploy log are all unreadable from here, and there is no workflow_dispatch. WHY I DID NOT JUST FORCE IT: 69a1385 modifies nginx/nginx.conf, which the brief names as an escalate-only file, and that same nginx change is what sets backend=true in deploy.yml and selects the --no-cache rebuild branch, which is the likeliest place for the failure to live. Pushing blind retries at an infrastructure change I am not allowed to author is guessing. WHAT YOU NEED TO DO: open the Actions run for 69a1385 and read which step failed. Most likely candidates from reading deploy.yml are the Crane Cab stamp step (it is designed to fail the deploy rather than ship a build claiming to be dev), the frontend build, or the backend verify step that checks the container restarted. ONE IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this run pushed state.json, whose deploy has BEFORE=0e2c2c4 and therefore CHANGED=scripts/health/state.json alone, backend=false, frontend-only branch. That may land the synth frontend and bump sw.js to v69 while leaving the nginx /synth/ carve-out unapplied, so a working /synth/ tomorrow is NOT evidence the original deploy succeeded. Check the Actions history, not the symptom. UPDATE, SAME NIGHT, READ THIS BEFORE ACTING ON THE ABOVE. The gap is CLOSED and the caveat in the preceding paragraph was wrong. This routine's state.json push (115e634) brought production fully up to origin/main, and it was verified afterwards: /sw.js dxedge-v69, https://dxedge.net/synth/ serving 'Filament - a tube synthesizer - DXEdge', /api/health ok at 04:33:24Z, both standalone shells clean. The reason the earlier caveat was wrong is that deploy.yml's droplet step runs `git fetch origin main` + `git reset --hard origin/main` AND `docker compose restart nginx` UNCONDITIONALLY, with `nginx -t` validating afterwards; backend=false skips only `docker compose build backend` and `docker compose up -d`. Since 69a1385 changed no backend/ file and only tripped the ^nginx/ path regex, the frontend-only branch was sufficient to deploy it completely, nginx carve-out included. SO THE REMAINING QUESTION IS NARROW: why did 69a1385's own run fail or never start, when the pipeline worked 20 minutes later? The distinguishing factor is that 69a1385 took the backend=true branch, so the suspects are `docker compose build backend` (a --no-cache style rebuild), `docker compose up -d`, or the backend-restart verify step that greps `docker compose ps backend` - plus the possibility that the Actions run never started at all. Open the Actions history for 69a1385 and read which step went red. Low urgency, but every future backend or nginx change takes that same branch.

awaiting_james.priority: MEDIUM and the highest-value new finding since solar-sfi-monthly-dataset. Unlike most open items this is a real logic defect in backend code that produces wrong data on the dashboard, not a link, a label or an advisory. It is cosmetic in the sense that nothing crashes, but it misinforms operators about which mode a contest runs, which is core to what the dashboard is for. Timely: the worst-affected entry is 5 days out.
awaiting_james.detail: backend/contests.py enrich_contest() (line 54) returns the FIRST MAJOR_CONTESTS key that appears as a substring of the lowercased contest name, iterating in dict insertion order. The table mixes specific contest keys with broad generic ones, and the generic keys sit early, so they shadow both the specific curated entries and the name-based mode inference in the fallback at lines 61-65, which is only ever reached when NO key matches. CONFIRMED WRONG in tonight live /api/contests, 4 of 36 entries: (1) "CQ Worldwide DX Contest, SSB", Oct 24-25, 5 days away, returns mode CW, tier 2, sponsor Various, matched via the generic key "dx contest". It is an SSB contest. (2) "ARRL International DX Contest, SSB" likewise returns mode CW tier 2 via "dx contest" (verified offline against the real function, not in tonight window). (3) "NCCC FT4 Sprint", Oct 23, returns mode CW via the generic key "sprint", shadowing the "ft4" key that sits later in the table. It is an FT4 contest. (4) "RSGB 80m Autumn Series, SSB", Oct 22, returns mode Various via the generic key "80m", even though the fallback would have inferred SSB correctly from the name. SHARPEST CONSEQUENCE, worth more than the mode errors themselves: the curated tier-1 entries for the two biggest DX contests of the year are DEAD CODE and can never match. The table keys are "cq ww dx" and "arrl dx" with mode CW/SSB, sponsor CQ Magazine / ARRL and tier 1, but contestcalendar.com spells the names out as "CQ Worldwide DX Contest" and "ARRL International DX Contest", in which neither "cq ww dx" nor "arrl dx" is a contiguous substring. So the flagship contests are permanently served the generic tier-2 CW metadata instead of the tier-1 metadata James curated for them. If tier drives prominence or sorting anywhere in the frontend, they are also being under-ranked. VERIFICATION METHOD: MAJOR_CONTESTS was extracted with ast.literal_eval and enrich_contest reimplemented verbatim offline (backend/contests.py imports aiohttp, absent from this container), then run against tonight real names from /api/contests. Each mislabelled entry was traced to the exact shadowing key. The live API output and the offline reproduction agree on all 4. NOT FIXED, deliberately, on three independent grounds: it is none of the four autonomous repair categories (not link rot, not a redirect, not a deprecated feed endpoint, not an /api/feed bypass); changing mode and tier values is squarely a data-semantics change, which the brief lists under DO NOT fix autonomously; and the right fix is a design choice on James own curated reference table, not a mechanical repair. OPTIONS, in rough order of robustness: (a) match the LONGEST matching key rather than the first, which fixes all four cases at once without touching any data, since "cq worldwide dx" style specific keys would then win over "dx contest" - but it needs the specific keys to actually match, so pair it with (b); (b) correct the specific keys to the spellings contestcalendar actually emits, i.e. "cq worldwide dx" and "arrl international dx", which revives the dead tier-1 entries; (c) split the table into specific contests and generic fallbacks, consult specific first and only then generic, and let the name-based mode inference run BEFORE the generic table so "NCCC FT4 Sprint" and "RSGB 80m ... SSB" resolve from their own names; (d) drop the broad keys "dx contest", "sprint" and "80m" entirely and let the lines 61-65 inference handle those, which is the smallest diff but loses the sponsor and tier hints; (e) leave it, if the mode field is understood to be a rough hint. A nightly run should NOT pick among these. Needs James decision, and if he wants it applied he should say which option.
